mediaplanr.viz

Web charts for mediaplanr plans: the subplan tree, who owns which cell, how a backed cell adds up, and where a scenario came from.

The spec is the product

Every function returns a spec — a plain R list holding an Apache ECharts option. Not a widget, not a plot object.

library(mediaplanr)
library(mediaplanr.viz)

topline <- media_plan_from_df(
  data.frame(week = as.Date("2026-07-06"), channel = c("TV", "Search"),
             planned_spend = c(100000, 40000)),
  grain = "channel", time = "week", name = "Q3 topline"
)
tv <- media_plan_from_df(
  data.frame(week = as.Date("2026-07-06"), channel = "TV",
             partner = c("NBC", "ESPN"),
             planned_spend = c(70000, 50000)),
  grain = c("channel", "partner"), time = "week", name = "TV detail"
)

spec <- ec_tree(attach_subplan(topline, tv))
spec
#> <mediaplanr_spec> tree
#>   from    subplan_map()
#>   series  1
#>   size    2,505 bytes of JSON

as_widget(spec)   # draw it, in Shiny or a notebook
as_json(spec)     # send it, to anything that speaks JSON

That indirection is the point. The same list renders in Shiny, is returned from an LLM tool call and drawn by a frontend that has never run R, sits in a file next to plan_to_json() output, and can be read — or edited — by anything that speaks JSON. Nothing in a spec is a JavaScript callback: every label and tooltip is formatted in R and travels as a literal string.

It draws projections, not plans

mediaplanr owns the data work and exports it as projections — subplan_map(), ownership_map(), lineage(), compare_scenarios(), calendarize(), roll_up(). This package only ever reads those, never a plan’s @data. So a change to the plan model surfaces as a change to one table rather than to seven charts, and every function takes the projection directly when you already have one in hand:

ec_tree(plan)                 # convenience
ec_tree(subplan_map(plan))    # the same spec, from the table

If a picture needs a fact the projections do not carry, the fact belongs upstream. ownership_map() arrived in mediaplanr exactly that way.

What it draws

ec_tree() The subplan tree: each node a plan, each edge the cell it backs
tbl_tree() The same tree as a sortable table, with lock markers and spend bars
ec_ownership() Line items × weeks, coloured by who owns the number
ec_sunburst() Spend by nesting, one ring per level
ec_rollup() How one backed cell adds up — the reconciliation view
ec_compare() How spend moves across a set of scenarios
ec_lineage() Where each scenario came from, and what it cost to get there

Colour carries meaning and the roles stay apart: an accent for the plan’s own marks, an owner ramp so one subplan is one colour in every chart, and status colours reserved for mediaplanr::status_levels(). Pass theme = "dark", or a list of overrides, to any of them — the package ships no client’s palette.

See vignette("gallery") for all seven on one worked plan.

Installation 

# install.packages("pak")
pak::pak("Roeh-Marketing/mediaplanr.viz")
